chunks: Abu Ali Al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, from Safwan, from Musa ibn Bakr, from Zurara, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

When you shoot (an arrow), so you find it, and there are not traces of other than the arrow, and you see that it has not been killed by other than your arrow, so eat, whether it had disappeared from you or not disappeared from you.
ai.seo_question: What are the conditions for an arrow-killed animal to be considered halal in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi establishes the principle of *istishab* (presumption of continuity) in hunting, where the hunter's confidence (*ghalabat al-zann*) in his arrow being the sole cause of death validates the meat's permissibility. It highlights the Shia juristic reliance on the hunter's subjective certainty when objective verification is impossible, distinguishing it from cases where other signs of death might appear. This ruling underscores the practical ease granted to believers in acquiring lawful sustenance through hunting.
